item.title: What Is PHP? Why Are Government and Business Websites Going Offline?
item.description:
Governments and companies around the world are racing to patch their websites — or taking them offline until they can be fixed — after the discovery of major security flaws in PHP, a piece of software that underpins much of the internet.

OpenAI, whose artificial intelligence models were used to find the bugs, said in a blog post that it was “one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory” given PHP’s widespread use.

PHP, short for PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor, is a decades-old, open-source programming language that is used to build and run web applications. By some estimates, about 70 percent of all websites and web applications use the software.

Services in which PHP is a core ingredient include content management systems like WordPress and Drupal, which help people run websites. Because PHP is a sort of foundational code baked into so many platforms — think of it as invisible digital infrastructure — many businesses may not even realize they rely on PHP.

Security researchers discovered issues in the programming language that could be exploited by an outside attacker.

The bug, which has been hidden in the software for years, was identified by researchers at Calif, a small, U.S.-based cybersecurity company, using OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol model. Researchers from Wiz, an Israeli-American security firm owned by Google, also independently reported the vulnerabilities.

The flaw is the latest to be discovered using advanced A.I. tools, which cybersecurity experts have warned are dangerously effective at finding bugs and weaponizing them. In its blog post, OpenAI said that the discovery of the PHP vulnerability highlighted “how A.I. can uncover security flaws with internet-scale impact, but the same capabilities can also help attackers rapidly develop offensive tools and exploits.”

The company added that, as far as it was aware, “frontier A.I. found these vulnerabilities before attackers did.”

Given that PHP powers much of the web, security professionals are concerned that hackers could move quickly against unpatched systems, manipulating how they operate and stealing the private data they contain. Experts also cautioned that because the technical details are now public, malicious actors can reverse-engineer a patch to rapidly increase their attempts exploit the vulnerability.

That creates an unusually urgent race to update systems. While A.I. models can help spot vulnerabilities, it can also be used to target many victims at once.

The PHP disclosure was further complicated by a leak before the patch. On Tuesday, details of the bugs were mentioned in a post on a hacker forum, which prompted the nonprofit foundation that oversees the software to release a fix a day earlier than planned.

The defenders and hackers began racing to protect or compromise systems on Wednesday when the patch was released. But there were signs of an earlier leak from the group of security researchers working to create the fix.

Late Wednesday, Amazon revealed in a blog post that it had data showing that an unknown actor had used the PHP attack four days before the patch’s release against a honeypot network, or a decoy system, that the company maintains. (A honeypot network tries to catch cybercriminals in the act of doing something nefarious.)

The identity of the attacker was unknown, but the early activity suggested that hackers could have been readying attacks for days before a fix was released.

“It remains unclear how the actor acquired exploit information prior to disclosure,” C.J. Moses, the chief information security officer at Amazon, said in the blog post.

Sites that rely on PHP are vulnerable, which means a good chunk of the internet.

Matthew Prince, the chief executive of CloudFlare, which helps websites secure and manage internet traffic, said in a social media post on Wednesday that the company “saw thousands of attempts to exploit” the flaw in the hours before it was publicly announced.

“That jumped to tens of thousands in the 45 minutes post announcement, hundreds of thousands within 2 hours, and millions now,” Mr. Prince added.

Several government websites in Europe and Asia went offline as a precautionary measure.

The Dutch cybersecurity agency, Internet Archive and the operator of Wikipedia took down a number of its systems. In Britain, the prime minister’s office said some government services might be offline on Friday.

On Thursday morning, the website of Finland’s government displayed a message to users: “The websites of the government are fully or partially unavailable. We are currently resolving the issue. Please try again in a moment.”

Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi of Japan urged operators whose sites rely on PHP to apply the patch as soon as possible. For those unable to do so immediately, she wrote on social media, temporarily suspending websites and similar measures could be effective in reducing risk.

Because PHP is so pervasive, the collateral damage could fall on everyday users whose personal data and essential online services depend on sites staying secure. Consumers could experience online disruptions in the coming days with certain businesses or government services.

Aaron Krolik contributed reporting.

item.title: A Cancer Revolution
item.description:
Last week, we learned that Pope Leo XIV was diagnosed with lung cancer. This week, we learned that surgery removed the cancer entirely and he wouldn’t need further treatment.

Not so long ago, a lung cancer diagnosis would have been an automatic death sentence. It’s still deadly. But screening and a revolution in cancer treatments have radically reduced death rates. That’s good news, since rising life expectancies mean that many of us will get some type of cancer at some point in our lives. Worldwide, about one in five people will get cancer. In some rich countries, it is more like one in two.

I had a fascinating conversation with my colleague Nina Agrawal, a health reporter who has been following these breakthroughs closely. We covered a lot of ground, including the tantalizing prospect of a cancer vaccine.

Nina, the pope is recovering from lung cancer surgery. Lung cancer is particularly scary. But it’s a very different diagnosis than it would have been in the past.

Absolutely. There’s been a lot of progress. The mortality rate for lung cancer has fallen and the five-year survival rate — the portion of people who are still alive five years after being diagnosed — has doubled in the United States, from about 15 percent in the late 1990s to around 30 percent now. It’s still not great compared with other types of cancer; lung cancer remains the leading cause of cancer death.

Wow. So what has changed in cancer treatment?

Advances vary by cancer. In lung cancer, for example, a big one is targeted therapy. Many patients have a specific mutation — often in a gene called EGFR — and drugs that target that mutation have improved steadily over the last 20 years. That’s been a real game changer. Targeted therapy, as the name implies, acts specifically on cancer cells and mostly leaves healthy cells alone, whereas traditional chemotherapy is toxic to most cells, including healthy ones.

Breast cancer is another beneficiary of targeted therapy. This is the most common cancer among women; about one in eight American women get it. But survival rates are now much higher. That’s because screening has gotten better, as have treatments: in addition to targeted therapies, there are also new immunotherapies that activate the patient’s immune system to attack the cancer. Those didn’t exist 15 years ago.

Why are we seeing all these breakthroughs now?

Two big things have happened. One is genetic sequencing. Doctors can sequence an individual tumor, find its mutations and then tailor a treatment that specifically targets those mutations. For certain cancers, like some types of breast cancer, it can also tell you whether a patient is likely to benefit from chemotherapy, which can spare a lot of people that toxicity.

The other thing that’s really helped is understanding how the immune system can be harnessed to fight cancer. Researchers have figured out how to better use our own immune system to attack cancer cells. They’ve developed drugs that essentially take the brakes off certain cells in the immune system. Advanced melanoma, for example, used to be almost universally deadly. It’s been totally transformed since this class of immunotherapies was first approved in 2011.

And how widely are these new treatments available?

In the U.S., where a lot of this research happens, the treatments that are approved are generally covered to some degree by insurance. But even insured patients can still face bills that bankrupt them. Then you have the more experimental treatments that are not yet approved and harder to come by.

A new pancreatic cancer drug, for example, which targets a mutation common in many cancers, is now covered in the U.S., though the supply chain is still working itself out. The next generation is available only through clinical trials.

What about elsewhere in the world?

Globally, it varies. Targeted lung cancer therapies are more accessible in high-income Asian countries like Taiwan, but poorer countries bear a higher burden of cancer deaths, partly because of scarce access. The drug companies themselves decide which countries to seek drug approval from, and they often don’t apply in countries where they think they won’t make a lot of money.

You’ve written about some of the unexpected repercussions of people being diagnosed with cancer now living much longer. It’s been mostly good, but also sometimes complicated.

The patients I’ve spoken with are all grateful for the time. Stage 4 breast or lung cancer used to mean a maximum of a few years. Now some people live 10 or 12 years with that diagnosis. But that also makes it very hard to plan.

One woman I talked to was diagnosed with stage 4 lung cancer about six years ago. In her first year, she lived in 12-week increments, until her next scan. It’s very hard to plan your life three months or even six months at a time. Do you spend money or save it? Quit your job and travel?

Nina, will there ever be a cure for cancer?

We are still a long way from that. But researchers do talk about a cure now in a way they didn’t used to — and some cancers are becoming more like chronic diseases. But many advanced cancers still have limited treatments.

One exciting thing many are watching now is personalized cancer vaccines that can help prevent recurrence. We can already vaccinate against infections that cause cancer, like HPV. But now we’ve had the first big trial for a vaccine to prevent cancer recurring in patients with melanoma who had their tumors surgically removed. The full results were announced yesterday. The vaccine trains the immune system to recognize the cancer cell and then attack it. The hope, of course, is that these vaccines can be generalized to other cancers. But we’re not there yet.

France banned some protests in an attempt to avoid a repeat of the riots that rocked the country last weekend. Officials are pressing resale platforms like eBay to remove listings for looted items. Art Basel Paris will be cut short.

A Houthi strike on a major airport in Saudi Arabia near the center of the country’s oil industry killed at least two people. Oil prices jumped on the news, along with attacks on several commercial ships in the Gulf.

The U.S. and Israeli militaries have developed specific plans for renewed strikes against Iran after the Nov. 3 midterm elections, according to U.S. officials and other people briefed on the deliberations.

Researchers used A.I. to find a major online security flaw, forcing governments and companies to shut down many websites for repair.

Almost all of the world’s shallow-water coral reefs are critically endangered, a global group of scientists said.

Protesters in Indonesia demanded action to stop rainforest fires causing a haze that is making people sick.

The Ebola epidemic that began in the Democratic Republic of Congo has reached Nigeria and Kenya — the widest footprint of any Ebola outbreak to date.

The economy is a top concern for voters in the midterm elections. Our chief economic correspondent, Ben Casselman, explains in the video below how that could translate into losses for President Trump’s Republican Party.

A southern cassowary at an Australian zoo laid fluorescent green eggs there for the first time in 34 years.

The most clicked link in your newsletter yesterday was about dark nutrition.

Take a minute to read this short poem by Emily Dickinson. In just 50 words and three stanzas, she works her way through a single, elaborate metaphor about what is and what might be.

The mayor of Taipei, Chiang Wan-an, has declared a “typhoon day off” as Taiwan braces for Typhoon Champi. The decision did not come as a surprise: In Taiwan, typhoons can affect a politician’s re-election chances.

Chiang faces a vote next month, and typhoon days off are popular. If the storm turns out to be weaker, many will go shopping, to the movies or to sing karaoke. Read more about Taipei’s typhoon days.

Postpartum modeling: Barbara Palvin walked the Victoria’s Secret runway six weeks after giving birth, igniting a debate about maternity leave in America.

The war on rats: New York City is using a new gas-powered killing machine in its eternal battle against rodents.

Abracadabra: Harry Houdini, who died 100 years ago next week, is thought to have succumbed to appendicitis. But an alternative theory involves chop suey.

Kalakand is a chewy, milky dessert made by cooking milk and sugar until the milk almost solidifies. This version uses a shortcut to make the no-bake dessert, or mithai, found in South Asian sweet shops.

Where is this riverside town?

Sevnica, Slovenia

Dürnstein, Austria

Qunu, South Africa

Elmina, Ghana

This week we took our children to visit Aberfan, a former coal mining town in Wales. Sixty years ago this week, a black avalanche of coal slurry tore down a hillside into Aberfan’s primary school, killing 116 children and 28 adults.

At the school assembly that day, they had sung “All Things Bright and Beautiful” and were about to start class when it happened. Most of the children who died were between 7 and 10 years old. (My son is 10. I hugged him a lot this week.)

Aberfan is a shared national tragedy in Wales. It’s a term that conjures tears in grown men two generations on.

National tragedies involving the deaths of children resonate especially deeply. Like the 2008 Sichuan earthquake in China, when more than 5,000 children died in collapsed schools. Or the Sewol ferry disaster, which claimed the lives of 250 school children in South Korea in 2014. In the U.S., school shootings have become associated with names like Sandy Hook and Columbine.

These are very different tragedies, but all of them involve a raw sense of futility and injustice. At the inquest in Aberfan, when a child’s cause of death was listed as asphyxia and multiple injuries, one father memorably said: “No, sir. Buried alive by the National Coal Board. That is what I want to see on the record.”

One episode of the Netflix drama “The Crown” focuses on Aberfan (Season 3, Episode 3). It’s very powerful. I rewatched it this week. Here’s a scene from the funeral, but the whole hour is worth it.

I can’t give you a happy song today. But a beautiful one, one that Karl Jenkins composed for the 50th anniversary of the Aberfan disaster. Here is “Lament for the Valley.” Sit with it.

Have a good weekend. — Katrin

item.title: Above Iran’s Capital, a Trump Impersonator Dances in a Jail Cell
item.description:
Mounted above one of Tehran’s busiest squares and affixed to a billboard is a cage designed to look like a jail cell. Inside it is an impersonator of President Trump. He rattles the bars, naps on his cell bed and mimics his famed Y.M.C.A. dance.

He does anything, that is, but look at the images flashing on the electronic billboard behind him, which depict a deadly American attack that struck an Iranian wedding last month.

“Failure to see this scene is a crime,” one of the scrolling images says, as rolls of yellow crime scene tape unfurl across the screen.

The piece of propagandistic performance art is one of the most eccentric in the Islamic republic’s long history of using billboards around the capital, Tehran, as a messaging tool.

Those messages reached new heights of provocation after the United States and Israel attacked Iran in February. Over the summer, for example, a billboard in Tehran’s central Enghelab Square showed an image of Mr. Trump lying in a graffitied coffin.

Mr. Trump has himself been an enthusiastic purveyor of politicized and ominous messaging to Iran. He has posted images on social media, usually generated using artificial intelligence, that mock Iran’s clerical rulers or depict their annihilation by American firepower.

Throughout the war, Iran’s government and its supporters have produced comedic memes and videos online that skewer the U.S. president and his decision to attack Iran.

Lego-styled music videos, mocking Trump administration officials, have frequently gone viral. Analysts said the videos, made by an anonymous group of content creators called “Explosive Media,” often attracted more interest abroad than inside the country.

Yet the Islamic republic’s latest gimmick — using a live actor in mask and wig to mimic Mr. Trump while marking a deadly attack — has grabbed public attention, even among Iranians who often walk right past such imagery on their streets.

Though the population is deeply divided in its feeling toward the regime, especially after a brutal crackdown on nationwide protests in January, there is widespread anger toward the U.S. leader for launching a devastating war on Iran.

International news agencies have published video reports showing the masked actor gesticulating to the crowd as he moves around his cell, which includes a bed, toilet and sink. Over the past few days, many have stopped to film, laugh and honk horns at the spectacle, mounted above an iconic square in one of the capital’s more affluent districts.

Tajrish Square, a bustling transportation hub in Tehran, is beloved among residents for its markets, where vendors sell nuts, fruits, clothing and gold. It is not a typical site for political statements, such as Enghelab Square, which means “Revolution Square” and is often the site of political gatherings and billboards.

The Trump performance, which has lasted into the night, was unveiled on Tuesday by Tehran’s Beautification Organization, affiliated with the city’s municipality, according to Iranian state media.

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the billboard. The installation appears to be part of a recently announced 15-day campaign in the capital intended to draw attention to the attack in the southern Iranian town of Kuhestak last month, in which at least one U.S. bomb hit a large wedding.

Asked about the attack at the time, U.S. Central Command, which coordinates American forces in the region, said that it was aware of Iranian news reports about the strike and that it doesn’t target civilians.

The wedding was struck by a bomb that, according to a weapons expert and a visual analysis by The New York Times, had been released by American forces as they carried out intense attacks in southern Iran.

For years, the Islamic republic struggled to make its anti-American messaging resonate beyond its hard-line base, said Omid Memarian, a senior Iran analyst at the Washington-based research group, DAWN.

“The war has altered that dynamic,” he said, with Iranians suffering days of bombardment and hearing Mr. Trump threaten to send Iran “back to the Stone Age.”

“The propaganda apparatus has gained renewed momentum,” Mr. Memarian said. “The message is that, despite America’s overwhelming military superiority, Iran is neither intimidated nor afraid to confront it.”

item.title: In Serbia’s Election, Identity Politics Looks to Be Winning Again
item.description:
Hunting for ways to rally voters, the media machine of Serbia’s embattled strongman Aleksandar Vucic has been accusing his rivals of smearing a notorious Serb general, who was convicted of genocide and crimes against humanity.

Ratko Mladic, who died in custody in The Hague in August, was the general behind the 1995 Srebrenica massacre in Bosnia. Yet many Serbs remember him as a valiant warrior who defended his people and their identity from attack by Bosnian Muslims seeking their own state.

Denying his crimes has become a note in Mr. Vucic’s campaign pitch, seen by his camp as a surefire way to stoke nationalist sentiment and win votes before the high-stakes general election on Oct. 25.

“Everyone in Serbia plays the same identity card,” said Vladimir Vuletic, a pro-Vucic sociology professor at Belgrade University. Most Serbs, he added, know that Mr. Mladic committed crimes. But Mr. Mladic was buried in Belgrade, Serbia’s capital, in September with military honors anyway.

“This is an identity problem, not a rational problem,” added Professor Vuletic, who noted that ethno-nationalist loyalties often trump reason.

Mr. Vucic has been Serbia’s dominant political figure since 2012, serving as both prime minister and president. He stepped down last month as head of state to lead the election campaign of his Serbian Progressive Party, rebranded for Sunday’s vote as “Aleksandar Vucic — United Serbia.”

If his party wins again, as many analysts expect given the lopsided playing field and wide scope for fraud, he will return as prime minister, his long hold on Serbia strengthened after nearly two years of sometimes huge protests against him led by students.

Student protesters selected their own slate of candidates for the election called “Student List — Students Win.” It includes no students but, according to some opinion polls, is running neck and neck with Mr. Vucic’s party.

Whatever the result, it is already clear that the enduring grip of nationalist identity politics is a powerful political tool.

For example, assailing the opposition as traitors, Informer, a Serbian tabloid that channels Mr. Vucic’s views, recently denounced his election rivals for hoisting a “scandalous banner.” Its message: “Gen. Ratko Mladic is a criminal.” Politika, another pro-Vucic outlet, said that by making such a claim, the opposition was “demonstrating its anti-Serb views.”

Student protesters, eager to avoid being branded unpatriotic, in May issued a “Memorandum on Kosovo and Metohija,” using the Serbian name for territory that, since 2008, has been an independent state. It rhapsodized over “the blood-soaked battlefield” and vowed to never surrender what it described as “not merely territory” but “a component of Serbian national identity.”

Long before Donald J. Trump entered politics promising to put “America first” and Marine Le Pen of France and other right-wing European populists surged on pledges to defend “native-born” citizens against “others,” Serbia and its neighbors put ethno-nationalism at the forefront of politics. They continue to do so.

That has helped lock Serbia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, North Macedonia and Kosovo, four countries that emerged from the wreckage of war in former Yugoslavia, in a decades-old political limbo.

Croatia and Slovenia, two other former parts of Yugoslavia, have also struggled with identity politics turbocharged by 1990s bloodshed but curbed them enough to win admission to the European Union.

Wartime ethnic passions might have faded but, said Vladimir Arsenijevic, a Serbian novelist, “the 1990s are still breathing down all our necks.”

The rank breath of that decade is especially strong in places like Krusevac, Serbia’s capital in the 14th century and a bastion of support for Mr. Vucic in the center of the country. The city was heavily bombed by NATO warplanes in 1999 during the conflict over Kosovo.

A big statue in the center of town honors a revered local hero, Prince Lazar, a Serb leader who died leading a Christian army to confront advancing Ottoman forces in Kosovo in 1389.

“We will never accept that Kosovo is not part of Serbia,” said Milos Nenezic, the general director of Krusevac’s biggest employer, Trayal Corporation, a state-controlled company with more than 1,000 employees. It got its start making explosives and now focuses on car tires.

Thanks to Mr. Vucic, he said, his factory has recovered from a disastrous privatization that had pushed it toward bankruptcy.

With new city streets, a new highway to Belgrade, a new hospital and many other improvements that Mr. Nenezic credits to Mr. Vucic’s policies, Krusevac highlights the twin pillars of what the government hopes is a winning election formula: robust patriotism and economic growth that could reach nearly 4 percent this year.

That is more than double the pace in neighboring Hungary, where the longtime leader Viktor Orban, a close ally of Mr. Vucic’s and fellow nationalist, lost an April election by a wide margin.

Srdjan Gasic, 34, a Krusevac resident who now works in finance, said he left his hometown in 2011 to study in Switzerland because the city felt “like a tomb.” Returning after Mr. Vucic took power, he found Krusevac “completely changed,” its potholed streets repaved and crumbling apartment buildings renovated.

Not everyone is rooting for Mr. Vucic, although openly siding with the student protesters who oppose him comes with heavy risks because of the governing party’s tight grip on the city. Danijel Ivanovic, a physical education teacher, said he lost his job last year at a local high school after joining protest marches. “I was fired because I had a different political view,” he said.

Yet he has no quarrel with Mr. Vucic’s nationalism and said the claims that the protesters “are not real Serbs” and think that Mr. Mladic was a criminal “are just lies” aimed at tricking voters into supporting Mr. Vucic.

The protest movement, a loose alliance of diverse political views with no clear leader, has stirred unease among some Serbs who want their country to make a clear choice in favor of the European Union.

Historically Serbia has deep ties to Russia, linked by a shared Orthodox faith and close economic and diplomatic relations.

Mr. Arsenijevic, the novelist, said he initially had high hopes for the student-led protests when they began in 2024 amid a wave of public anger at the death of 16 people killed by falling concrete at a newly renovated railway station. But, he added, he was aghast when the protesters, too, started embracing nationalist themes and symbols.

Serbia, its halfhearted ambitions to join the European Union stalled and its dream of recovering Kosovo seemingly doomed but still loudly proclaimed, “seems completely lost in time and space,” Mr. Arsenijevic added.

In 2009 he founded a group he still heads called Krokodil, which promotes cultural exchange and reconciliation between former Yugoslav peoples.

He is a frequent target of death threats and in July was badly beaten in Belgrade by young nationalist thugs who accused him of betraying Serb interests. His group’s activities include painting over graffiti that hail Gen. Mladic as a “hero” and President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia as Serbia’s only true friend.

Violent thugs, he added, “are just a fringe” but their view that Serbia has been unfairly victimized and must stand up against foreign pressure over war criminals and Russia “represents just about everyone in society.”

The Student List, the strongest rival to Mr. Vucic’s party in Sunday’s general election, recently announced that it wants to continue the current government’s policy of resisting pressure from the European Union to impose sanctions on Moscow.

Nonetheless the Student List candidates are regularly tarred as traitors working for Croatia and Serbia’s other enemies in the 1990s, said Zoran Gavrilovic, the executive director of Birodi, an independent group that monitors Serbian media.

“Claiming that Mladic is not a criminal and that Kosovo is part of Serbia is a lie, but it wins votes,” Mr. Gavrilovic, a sociologist, said, because of the Vucic camp’s ability to stir up nationalist sentiment through its control of the media.

His data show that Mr. Vucic got 78 percent of the total airtime devoted to politics in September on Serbia’s five television stations that had a national reach. A further 13 percent went to his party.

Student-List candidates got only 6 percent of airtime while European Serbia, the only party openly pushing for entry to the E.U., was given less than 1 percent.

Milan Protic, a historian who was mayor of Belgrade after the fall of Serbia’s wartime leader Slobodan Milosevic in 2000, said “decades of brainwashing” had left many Serbs convinced that “if you say anything” against nationalist narratives “you are a traitor and anti-Serb.”

Most Serbs, he added, “know nothing of their history” because the topic was suppressed under Josip Broz Tito, Yugoslavia’s longtime communist dictator, and then hijacked by opportunist party apparatchiks like Mr. Milosevic when the Yugoslav multiethnic state disintegrated.

“The only thing they know about is the Battle of Kosovo,” Mr. Protic said, referring to the 1389 battle. The 600th anniversary of the battle, a taproot of Serb national identity, was used by Mr. Milosevic to stir up nationalist fervor that put Serbia on the road to war with its neighbors in the 1990s.

Kosovo, Mr. Gavrilovic, the media monitor, said, “is obviously now lost but nobody wants to hear this. They reject reality.”

Alisa Dogramadzievacontributed reporting.

item.title: Arms Race Intensifies in Korea as the North Is Emboldened by Russia Alliance
item.description:
An intensifying arms race is gripping the Korean Peninsula, as both sides trade missile tests and North Korea supercharges development of more lethal warheads, attack drones and other new weapons to threaten the South.

North and South Korea have maintained a fierce military rivalry since the Korean War ended in an uneasy armistice, with Pyongyang turning to nuclear weapons after the Soviet bloc collapsed. Now, North Korea is rapidly upgrading its conventional forces with the help of its military partnership with Russia, recently revitalized by the Ukraine war.

In exchange for North Korean arms and soldiers, Russia has given the North a live combat laboratory to test its weapons and troops, refine its missile performance and master drone warfare. The North’s military may soon be able to unleash vast swarms of low-cost drones to overwhelm the more expensive, high-tech defenses of South Korea and the U.S. forces stationed there.

Rising hostility along the inter-Korean border has given an ominous tone to the region’s military buildup. In recent months, North Korea has begun heavily fortifying its border with more powerful weapons and additional barbed-wire fences, concrete barriers and minefields.

Tensions escalated further after three South Korean soldiers were injured last month by North Korean land mines that Seoul says were buried south of the ill-defined border. The two Koreas have since traded warning shots and threats of military conflict.

Then, a rare tit-for-tat escalation this month exposed the increasingly lethal arsenals that the countries are amassing across their border, already the world’s most fortified.

Early this month, under the watch of its leader, Kim Jong-un, North Korea launched what it called a nuclear-capable ballistic missile from its east coast toward waters between Russia’s Far East and Japan’s northern island of Hokkaido.

Officials in South Korea and Japan estimated the missile traveled around 430 miles. But Pyongyang said it flew 621 miles. It ridiculed them for losing track of the warhead, claiming it performed sudden, irregular “wavelike” maneuvers while flying at several times the speed of sound — signature behaviors of a hypersonic missile. “This means there is no way to avoid this attack,” North Korea said.

According to Shin Jong-woo, secretary-general of the Korea Defense and Security Forum in Seoul, North Korea’s launch “was not a mere show of force, but a demonstration that the advancement of its hypersonic weapon system is in its final stage.”

South Korea usually responds to North Korean missile tests with brief statements condemning them as provocative. But five days after the North’s launch, it test-fired its own hypersonic ballistic missile for the first time, observed by President Lee Jae Myung, indicating that Seoul has grown increasingly uneasy over the rapid advancement of North Korea’s missile technology.

During North Korea’s hypersonic missile test, Mr. Kim urged the nation’s military to “repeatedly make the enemy recognize the reliability and fatality” of its weapons.

It has been able to make such strides thanks to valuable battlefield data and feedback acquired while helping Russia fight in Ukraine, said Anton Ponomarenko, a researcher at Pacific Forum who monitors Russia-North Korea military cooperation. He noted that improved accuracy and maneuverability of its warheads made the threat to South Korea “more substantial.”

Cooperation with Russia has also helped the North develop new drone capabilities. Pyongyang has learned from the conflict in Ukraine and the Middle East that inexpensive drones can overwhelm costly air-defense systems. During a North Korean drill last month, a drone swarm attacked a target island, while cruise and ballistic missiles struck simultaneously from different directions. North Korea’s evolving tactics will eventually force South Korea and its allies to redesign their air defenses at exorbitant costs, defense experts said.

The drone partnership has scaled rapidly. Russia has recruited 12,000 North Korean workers to its Geran-2 drone factories in Tatarstan while dispatching officers to North Korea to train drone operators, according to Ukrainian officials. A sanctions-monitoring group warned last month that Russia’s appetite for North Korean labor across various defense sectors raises the risk of vital military technology ending up in Pyongyang’s hands.

The consequences are already visible: Photos from Mr. Kim’s visit to a drone factory last month indicated that North Korea has begun mass-producing drones.

“We will see a deepening imbalance between low-cost attacks and high-cost defenses,” said Hong Min, an analyst at the Korea Institute for National Unification in Seoul.

Even before North Korea began receiving help from Russia, its military was working to make its weapons harder to target. It has tested missiles launched from submarines and mobile launchers hidden in tunnels. It also switched from liquid to solid fuel to drastically reduce missile launch preparation time.

As North Korea continues to improve its missiles, some of which can carry both conventional and nuclear warheads, “it will become extremely difficult for us to discern the nature of the warhead or the intent behind an attack based solely on the launch itself,” said Kim Yong-ho, a former director of strategic intelligence at the South Korean Defense Ministry.

South Korea still relies on the presence of U.S. military bases, and ultimately the American nuclear arsenal, as a deterrent against a nuclear attack. It has not sought to develop its own atomic weapons, but instead to offset the North’s growing strike capabilities by building up conventional arms to create what analysts call a balance of fear. That means strengthening its three-pronged strategy for responding to a potential attack: pre-emptive strikes, missile defense and massive retaliation.

On the day South Korea tested its first hypersonic missile, President Lee’s office released a photo of him inspecting another new weapon, the Hyunmoo-5 missile. Dubbed a “monster” by local media, it reportedly carries an eight-ton bunker-buster warhead that can penetrate shelters deep underground to kill enemy leaders.

During an interview with The New York Times last month, Mr. Lee described South Korea’s conventional retaliation capability as “probably one of the most capable in the world.”

“Even if North Korea possesses nuclear weapons, they would serve only as a last-resort defensive measure,” he said. “Using them offensively would ensure the North’s self-destruction.”

To monitor North Korean missile activity, South Korea operates reconnaissance aircraft and satellites in close coordination with the United States. Seoul also maintains air and naval superiority, while Pyongyang largely depends on aging Soviet-era aircraft and the capabilities of newly built destroyers remain unproven.

Like North Korea, South Korea has leveraged overseas conflicts to boost its defense industry. In June, Mr. Lee said that during the wars in Ukraine and Iran foreign leaders have rushed to secure South Korean air-defense missiles, with one country even sending a cargo plane to collect them directly from the production line.

Pyongyang ​put its first ​military spy satellite in orbit​ in 2023, although South Korean officials dismissed its technology as rudimentary. Yet North Korea is catching up in more areas, fueling a cat-and-mouse arms race.

Four days after Mr. Lee inspected the Hyunmoo-5, ​North Korea launched what analysts identified as a bunker-buster missile of its own, capable of carrying a 2.5-ton payload, unusually large for a short-range ballistic missile.

Defense analysts say North Korea has now surpassed South Korea in some capabilities. Some of the South Korean military’s recent drone tests ended in high-profile flops, with drones crashing shortly after takeoff.​ And North Korea unveiled the completed hull of what it called its first nuclear-powered submarine in December​, while South Korea is still negotiating with Washington to secure fuel for a similar vessel it hopes to build by the mid-2030s.

South Korea is reacting to the growing threat from the North by increasing military spending at a record pace. It has pledged to raise defense expenditures from 2.8 percent to 3.5 percent of gross domestic product, becoming the first American ally to adopt such a target amid Washington’s pressure on partners to reduce reliance on U.S. forces.

However, the greatest threat posed by the North might not even target South Korea. If Russia helped it develop an ability to strike the United States directly with nuclear warheads, this might make Washington think twice about coming to the South’s aid, said Lami Kim, a Korea chair at the London-based International Institute for Strategic Studies.

“This would undermine the credibility of U.S. extended deterrence, as Washington would face the prospect of risking nuclear strikes against American cities to defend South Korea,” she said.

item.title: Powerful Earthquake Kills at Least 16 People in Tibet
item.description:
A 7.0-magnitude earthquake struck China’s southwestern region of Tibet on Thursday, killing at least 16 people and sending others fleeing outdoors, according to Chinese state media.

The earthquake hit at 10:33 p.m. local time around 119 miles from the city of Nagqu in northern Tibet, according to the U.S. Geological Survey. Several subsequent tremors were reported in the region. The quake left at least 65 people injured and destroyed more than 300 homes, state media reported.

Video footage released by China’s state broadcaster showed dozens of people running from stores, restaurants and apartment buildings as the quake shook the ground. Soldiers and rescue workers were also shown loading water and food supplies onto military trucks and driving along a narrow road to reach the affected area.

As of 10 a.m. on Friday, 12,489 people had been safely evacuated, according to the state news agency Xinhua.

The quake disrupted water and electricity for residents living in villages around Maru township, the epicenter of the earthquake. There are around 7,605 residents in Maru, according to a 2020 census.

More than 1,600 search and rescue workers have been sent to the city of Nagqu, the official Chinese news agency, Xinhua, reported. Eleven of those injured were seriously hurt. At least one person trapped under rubble was successfully rescued.

View the location of the quake’s epicenter and shake area.

Xi Jinping, China’s leader, called for “intensified effort” by rescue workers and urged officials to continue to monitor the situation and weather in the area, which is at a high altitude where the air is cold and snow is expected in the coming days.

Nagqu is around 300 miles from Lhasa, the capital of Tibet. Annexed by Beijing in the 1950s, Tibet is tightly surveilled and has been a place of protest, including self-immolations, by Tibetans who have long fought to maintain their religious freedom and cultural identity, which is separate from the majority Han Chinese.

It is also one of the most underdeveloped parts of China, with many areas difficult to reach. Deadly floods that swept through another part of Tibet in September killed at least dozens in Tibet and 1,300 people in Nepal.

The Himalayan region has recorded powerful earthquakes in the recent past. A magnitude-7.8 earthquake in Nepal in 2015 killed nearly 9,000 people.

Murphy Zhao contributed reporting.

item.title: Converting Ebola Skeptics: Christian Leaders Mobilize Communities in Congo
item.description:
Deo Kasereka said he could pinpoint the moment he was infected with Ebola. As a catechist at the Notre Dame of Maternal Charity church in Mongbwalu, Democratic Republic of Congo, it was his job to comfort the sick, he said.

When he attended the funeral of a parishioner this summer, he touched the body, in keeping with traditional burial practices in Congo, he said. A few days later he started feeling ill. “I was feverish and so hot I couldn’t sleep. I was just sweating and coughing,” he said.

In the early days of the outbreak, many people say they did not know how to protect themselves against the virus. “If someone reached out their hand, I would take it,” Mr. Kasereka said.

But after Mr. Kasereka got sick, his daughter implored him to seek treatment at the new Ebola clinic. She knew the importance of early treatment, having helped respond to another Ebola outbreak in 2019 here in Mongbwalu, a remote town spread over steep green hills and surrounded by informal gold mines.

Four days after checking into the clinic and testing positive for Ebola, Mr. Kasereka was released when he got a negative test. He credits his daughter for his recovery. “Because my family was well informed, I got treatment early,” he said. “But if you wait, and come after vomiting and diarrhea has started, it’s usually too late.”

Mr. Kasereka now uses his status as a low-level church official and an Ebola survivor to help spread the word about the importance of early treatment and to counter widespread claims that Ebola was invented by outsiders to kill local inhabitants and steal their mineral-rich land.

“People come up with mysterious justifications for illnesses when they don’t understand,” said the Rev. Richard Dieudonne Ivale, the priest in Mr. Kasereka’s parish.

The outbreak in Congo has killed at least 4,687 people since May, making it the fastest-spreading Ebola epidemic ever recorded. It has also reached its widest expansion ever, with cases in Uganda, Kenya and Nigeria. At least 346 Ebola patients have died at the Mongbwalu clinic. But health workers agree that infections are starting to decline here, in part because of the effective community outreach done by health workers as well as faith leaders.

“I can only give the medical message, and that may not always work, but priests are using their authority to convert that message into something spiritual, something related to the Bible,” said Dr. Marie Roseline Belizaire, a World Health Organization official in Africa. “I heard one priest give a sermon, and he referred to the commandment, ‘Thou shalt not kill.’ He said by not taking people who are sick to get treated, people were in effect killing them. That’s a very strong message.”

Congo has the largest Roman Catholic population in Africa, with around a third of the 117 million Congolese identifying as Catholic. The church is one of the few institutions with a functioning national infrastructure in the country. It provides social services such as hospitals and around half the nation’s schools, according to the Vatican.

The church also holds considerable influence over politics and daily life in a nation ravaged by decades of conflict.

During Mass at Notre Dame of Maternal Charity, congregants get hand sanitizer before receiving holy communion, while priests share the latest information about Ebola and remind their hundreds of parishioners to follow safe burial practices. (The Ebola virus is highly contagious after a victim dies, potentially infecting anyone who comes into contact with the body.)

Before a service in June, members of the choir sang to celebrate two young boys who had just recovered from the virus.

“We were the first to start informing people through our church and through our radio,” Father Ivale said. “We have communities spread out across the province, and we relayed truthful information for them to share. Now people have started to understand. There’s a big change. We’ve had to provide a lot of awareness so that the population believes Ebola exists.”

This was no small task.

The death of a Mongbwalu pastor in February most likely set off a superspreader event, well before the World Health Organization declared the outbreak an epidemic in May. Dozens from the community, including three close relatives, died within two weeks of his funeral.

The sudden wave of deaths and some circumstances of the pastor’s burial prompted rumors, misleading social media posts and even a song by a local band about a ghostly casket haunting the neighborhood and causing the illness.

To help counter such misinformation, as well as rumors that patients were being killed inside Ebola clinics and their organs harvested, Mr. Kasereka, the catechist who survived, has made regular appearances on popular church radio broadcasts to talk about Ebola. He has also ventured out into surrounding communities to speak with residents directly.

“Before I survived Ebola, people said not to go to hospital because it only meant death,” Mr. Kasereka said. “But when I was healed, by the grace of God, things started to change. I was an example that treatment can work.”

The Catholic Church is not alone in trying to dispel the misinformation. On a recent Sunday morning, inside the Vision of the Ladder Evangelical church in Mongbwalu, The Rev. Paul Kayongo was just getting warmed up.

Wearing a shiny jacket with a golden leaf pattern over his red clerical shirt, he danced, hips swaying and palms upturned, as women sang in Swahili. A guitarist, a drummer and a keyboardist played on instruments amplified by a generator that also powered a single fluorescent bulb above the pulpit.

Purple and silver bunting hung from the low plywood ceiling. Behind the preacher, multicolored curtains covered the mud walls.

A few dozen churchgoers danced and prayed as the music and song drifted out into the surrounding streets. The service lasted three hours, and culminated with Pastor Kayongo’s most pressing message: If there is one thing to believe in, aside from God, it’s that Ebola is real.

“This neighborhood is where it all started,” Pastor Kayongo said as he greeted passers-by in the streets after the service. “We didn’t know what was happening.”

“People here were just dying everywhere before the epidemic was even announced,” he said, pointing up a winding alleyway. “On this street alone, more than 80 people died in a few weeks. Now there is almost nobody left; they have all died or fled.”

Pastor Kayonga also works at Mongbwalu’s Ebola clinic, counseling family and friends of the sick or deceased. He has been in Mongbwalu from the start of the outbreak, which began here as early as January.

“It was terrible at that time,” he said. “It’s still bad, but without our efforts to inform people, things would be much worse.”

item.title: Gadi Eisenkot Couldn’t Be More Unlike Netanyahu. Can He Beat Him?
item.description:
Gadi Eisenkot doesn’t speak like a politician. He runs through his plans matter-of-factly, like a commander spelling out a mission to his troops.

It’s an unusual style of campaigning, and scarcely electrifying; he doesn’t so much appeal to voters as state what he sees as the obvious.

But for Mr. Eisenkot, a former Israeli military chief and the leading candidate against Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in Tuesday’s election, it reflects who he is, how he approaches leadership and how serious he believes Israel’s problems have become.

It also reflects the grief he felt as father to a son killed two months into Israel’s war in Gaza — grief that was on vivid display when he delivered a eulogy on national television.

Mr. Eisenkot, 66, says he is running to “save Israel.” In his view, Mr. Netanyahu has embroiled Israel in forever wars, destroyed its international standing and decimated its support in the United States. He’s pushed the country toward authoritarianism, Mr. Eisenkot argues, and turned segments of society against one another. Extremist Jews are marauding through Palestinian villages in the West Bank. Organized criminals are killing Arab citizens. Army reservists are called up again and again because ultra-Orthodox Israelis dodge the draft.

And Mr. Netanyahu has not accepted responsibility for the security failures that led to the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas-led attack.

It is the avoidance of responsibility that offends Mr. Eisenkot most.

When Israeli passengers overpowered the co-pilot of a FlyDubai jet who attacked the captain and tried to crash the plane, Mr. Eisenkot noted with disdain, Mr. Netanyahu milked the moment for a photo op. But when it became clear that Israeli security failures had nearly cost passengers their lives, he let underlings address the criticism.

Mr. Eisenkot now calls Mr. Netanyahu an “anti-leader.”

“I was taught, and it’s how I conducted myself throughout my military service: When things go well, put the people who made it happen out front,” he said on a podcast days later. “When things go wrong, step forward and take responsibility. This is the exact opposite of Netanyahu.”

“This election,” he told The Times of Israel, “is a choice between responsibility and running away from responsibility.”

The question, as Mr. Eisenkot’s lead over Mr. Netanyahu has dwindled, is whether Israelis will entrust someone who has served only part of one term as a lawmaker and eight months as a minister — and has never stood up to global pressure — with the country’s biggest responsibility of all.

Mr. Eisenkot, who is refusing interviews with foreign news organizations, could not be less like the incumbent.

Where Mr. Netanyahu grew up in Jerusalem’s Ashkenazi elite, Mr. Eisenkot is a product of Israel’s long-neglected periphery: born in Tiberias, in the north, to Moroccan immigrants; raised in working-class Eilat, in the south. He would be the first Mizrahi to become prime minister. That could help him: Mizrahim, descended from Middle Eastern or North African Jews, make up roughly half of Israel’s Jews and much of Mr. Netanyahu’s political base.

The two men also approach work very differently.

Mr. Netanyahu is known to drag out decisions and maneuver for immediate advantage. “He’d say Thursday that he’d annex the West Bank, to get good results in the Friday evening TV, and then Sunday he’d say, ‘There are some limits,’ or ‘I’ll do it next week,’” said Yoav Horowitz, Mr. Netanyahu’s chief of staff from 2016 to 2019, who is writing a plan for Mr. Eisenkot’s first 100 days. “This is the opposite of Gadi. Gadi looks and works strategically, even though sometimes it hurts him.”

Mr. Eisenkot, a career military officer, also has developed a reputation for straight talk.

Former Prime Minister Ehud Barak said that Mr. Eisenkot, whom Mr. Barak chose as his military secretary when he defeated Mr. Netanyahu in 1999, would restore “trust and truth” to the premier’s office.

“In this regard, Eisenkot is a towering figure compared to Netanyahu,” Mr. Barak said.

“And it’s a great Jewish tikkun” — a repair, or correction — “to everything Israel has done,” he added. “Gadi will not be so eloquent,” he said, but he will also “not be the person other leaders are recorded talking about as a liar.”

Nothing looms larger in what drives Mr. Eisenkot than his bereavement. In December 2023, the youngest of his five children, Gal, 25, a reservist, was killed in Gaza in a tunnel explosion. Thousands attended the funeral. Many more watched on TV as Mr. Eisenkot choked up eulogizing his son.

The day of the funeral, a nephew of Mr. Eisenkot’s was killed in Gaza. Another nephew was killed 11 months later.

Now, Mr. Eisenkot says in his raspy voice, he hopes to be “worthy of the enormous price paid” by his son. “So that there could be a better reality here for our children,” he said.

Rising through the ranks of the Golani Brigade, a gritty melting pot of an infantry unit, Mr. Eisenkot was known as a stickler for discipline.

As the brigade’s commander, he cracked down on misbehavior that had gone unaddressed for years. When one company rebelled, he told the Haaretz newspaper later, he sent dozens of soldiers to prison.

When he studied at the Army War College in Pennsylvania for a year in the 1990s, his wife, born in Hartford, Conn., started filling out applications for U.S. passports for their children. He tossed them in the trash. He suggested swimming lessons instead, since the kids would grow up in Israel — surrounded by past or present enemies — “with their backs to the sea.”

Mr. Eisenkot took command in the West Bank in 2003, at the height of the Second Intifada. Arresting Palestinian militants and speeding construction of a wall separating Israel from the West Bank, he helped stop the suicide bombings and end the uprising, according to Nitzan Alon, then a brigade commander, who said Mr. Eisenkot combined military capabilities and cooperation with the Palestinians “in a much more clever way.”

Palestinians in the West Bank interviewed by The New York Times did not specifically recall Mr. Eisenkot’s role in suppressing that uprising but described him as the far lesser of two evils when compared with Mr. Netanyahu.

Mr. Eisenkot also opposed right-wing calls for collective punishment of Palestinians for the acts of militants and, more broadly, argued for giving the Palestinians reason to hope for improved relations with Israel, including through political talks. “Someone who sees no light at the end of the tunnel will be quicker to light the fire,” he said in 2005.

He was harsher with Hezbollah. In 2008, he articulated the “Dahiya doctrine,” which called for creating deterrence by responding to attacks with devastation, as Israel did in the Dahiya suburb of Beirut in 2006, killing hundreds and displacing thousands.

In 2011, Mr. Barak, then defense minister, urged Mr. Netanyahu to name Mr. Eisenkot the military’s chief of staff over Benny Gantz, who was more senior. Mr. Eisenkot demurred, saying Mr. Gantz was more ready.

It was an unheard-of display of unselfishness among top generals known for jealousy and ambition. “I can’t fully explain it,” Mr. Barak said. “He didn’t question his own capability. He really just thought it was better for the army. It was noble behavior.”

Mr. Eisenkot did accept the top job in 2015, just as a wave of attacks began that killed dozens of Israelis. Some rabbis and politicians urged killing any attacker at the scene. But he warned soldiers to obey orders, not outsiders.

A month later, after a Palestinian stabbed an Israeli soldier and was quickly shot, a medic, Elor Azaria, walked up to the attacker, motionless on the ground, and shot him in the head — a killing captured on video.

Public sentiment heavily favored Mr. Azaria. But Mr. Eisenkot insisted that he be prosecuted. Despite angry protests, he stood by the military justice system, which sentenced Mr. Azaria to 18 months.

He has also politely declined repeated invitations to dine with Mr. Netanyahu, telling others he did not want a personal relationship to cloud his judgment.

And he stood his ground against what he saw as improper meddling. In 2017, when troops began the court-ordered evacuation of an illegal West Bank settlement, Mr. Netanyahu told Mr. Eisenkot to abort, according to two people briefed on the conversation who insisted on anonymity to discuss it. Mr. Eisenkot asked him to put the order in writing and get the attorney general to endorse it. Mr. Netanyahu backed down.

A Netanyahu spokesman did not respond to requests for comment.

“I probably wouldn’t have gotten to where I have in life without knowing how to be sophisticated, forceful when necessary and persuasive,” Mr. Eisenkot told one interviewer. “It didn’t happen because I was a nice person.”

Mr. Eisenkot’s time in Mr. Netanyahu’s current government was brief: He joined it, along with Mr. Gantz, five days after Oct. 7. He lasted eight months.

He describes Mr. Netanyahu as being unmoored by the attack, saying he was “shaking like a leaf.” But he lost patience with Mr. Netanyahu’s push for an elusive “total victory” over a deal with Hamas to release the hostages.

He resigned in June 2024. Last year, he formed a new party, Yashar — Hebrew for “straight” or “honest.”

On the trail, he assures Israelis that he would form a state commission of inquiry into the failures on Oct. 7, which Mr. Netanyahu has refused to do. Such a commission, he says, should also examine his own actions as chief of staff.

He promises to root out what he calls “Jewish terrorists” in the West Bank, remove illegal outposts, lift Israel’s squeeze on the Palestinian Authority and reissue work permits for many Palestinians to enter Israel.

He would also halt efforts to annex the West Bank, with its roughly three million Palestinians.

Such views have prompted Mr. Netanyahu to tell right-wing Israelis that Mr. Eisenkot would allow the creation of a Palestinian state. He also argues that Mr. Eisenkot’s relative inexperience — and even his comparably poor English — would allow world leaders to push Israel around, whereas Mr. Netanyahu can boast of President Trump’s endorsement and longtime backing.

Mr. Eisenkot does not, however, see a Palestinian state on the horizon.

Mr. Eisenkot’s entire platform is meant to get Israel on a path to what he considers normalcy. It includes term limits for prime ministers; drafting the ultra-Orthodox; requiring math, English and science classes, even in religious schools; and writing what Israel has never had: a constitution.

He wants to heal the country, something he says can occur only once Mr. Netanyahu is gone.

All of that prompts supporters to nod their heads. But seldom does he bring crowds to their feet. In a stop at the crowded Levinsky Market in Tel Aviv, he was almost bashful, sipping coffee and chatting one on one. Many voters had no idea he was there.

Which may help explain why his lead over Mr. Netanyahu has narrowed.

Some voters worry that he may lack what has kept Mr. Netanyahu in power: the political “knife between the teeth,” an all-out determination to do what it takes to win.

“I think his campaign is too quiet,” Ahuva Kfir, 73, said at a rally in Haifa. “He needs to step on the gas a little more.”

Her husband, Amitai, 77, saw things differently. “We shouldn’t compare him to Bibi,” he said. “We need someone who will be serious, honest, decent, brave, intelligent. I think he’s exactly the person.”

Adam Rasgon and Amit Elkayam contributed reporting from Tel Aviv.
